messages.subject: Re: Suitability prediction and RSF questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fang,

Unlike AIC, AICc can potentially return infinite or NaN values if the number of parameters is not sufficiently larger than the number of data points (or effective-sample-size with rsf.fit). I suspect that is what you are getting, especially given that your species tends to have small effective sample sizes. I would try BIC and if that doesn't work, then please send me a minimal working example to check.

mean() is coded up to provide a meta-analytic model for the population (and I just pushed a fix for that function for when the individual models vary). But you shouldn't expect one best individual model for all individuals, because, all else equal, the sampling can differ.

rsf.select() can drop variables at the individual level, but mean() should then keep all of the variables in the individual selected models (though not all parameters will support estimation of the population variance). If that's not the case, then please send me a minimal working example to diagnose.

You can supply different rasters for the suitability predictions than you did for the model fitting... if that's what you are asking?

I haven't yet coded up the categorical regression to be smart at the population level. Currently, you need to manually select the same reference category for each individual. But that may not be possible if there is no single category that all individuals sample from. At some point, I need to code up the mean() function to automatically transform between reference categories. If you need that functionality now, then please let me know and I will prioritize it.

For the error, please send me a minimal working example and I will take a look at it.

Best,
Chris

>

> 1. Why does the mean() function automatically exclude variables?
> 2. Is there a way to specify the variables for suitability prediction?
> 3. The selection of categorical data (forest; please find below the output of summary(mean)) does not make sense to me. Why did it not select all with the same reference category (i.e., why not forest.1_0 but forest.0_1 here)?
>    - forest.3_0 (1/forest.3_0)
>    - forest.2_0 (1/forest.2_0)
>    - forest.0_1 (1/forest.0_1)
>
> Questions related to suitability()

> temp_suit <- suitability(R=R,

> I am sorry for so many questions. Any insights from you would be greatly appreciated. Thank you very much!

Hi Tyler,

If you run mean() on the outputs of rsf.select() then both the betas should be there and the population variation in the betas should be there (if supported). If they are not, then please send me a minimal working example to look at.

If you run mean() on the UDs, then the betas would not be included.

Best,
Chris

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2 is intermediate and 3 is significantly and substantially off (the white space between the empirical and theoretical CIs). These variograms do match up to the behavior you describe.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I agree that 4,5,6 look like they might be increasing, but variogram errors are autocorrelated, so you can't necessarily ascribe a trend to that, as its within the expected range of errors.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Chris
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > On Monday, October 16, 2023 at 4:10:47 PM UTC-4 nyhe...@yahoo.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Hello group,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I don't mean to overly belabor the topic, but I was wondering about the range residency status of a subset of forest birds that I tracked via traditional VHF this past summer. Most of the birds demonstrated bounded home ranges throughout the breeding season with the variograms reaching obvious asymptotes, while others have variograms that are a bit questionable. Specifically, these birds had space use that changed slightly during different periods of the season, whereas the other birds had home ranges that remained static during the same time periods. As expected, the variograms for these birds are not typical, although for one of the birds with the least static whole-season space use (see discussion below), an asymptote does seem apparent. I am trying to get a handle on whether a full season analysis may be possible and appropriate with these birds, and if a mean breeding season home range size would be usable to inform other aspects of the study and analysis (e.g., I want to use the mean home range size to create a biologically meaningful buffer distance in which to summarize habitat covariates for point-counts conducted on the same study sites). Below, I share the questionable variograms and briefly discuss each bird's space use.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Note: When I refer to "movements", these are often only on the scale of a few hundred meters.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I was able to track this bird almost throughout the entire breeding season. At the beginning of the season, it had fairly static space use and was restricted to a small area, but during the post-fledging period its area of space use expanded greatly, and it was often found a few hundred meters from the area of original use. Then, during the post-breeding period, it briefly returned to its original area of use before settling in an area not too far from its original location. Despite this variable space use, however, the variogram seems rather stable.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 2
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > This bird had a very similar space use history to bird 1, with it occupying a fairly static area for much of the season, briefly moving away from this area during the post-fledging period, and then returning to the original location during the post-breeding period. However, rather the apparent asymptote of the first bird, this one has a distinct bell shape.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 3
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > This bird also has a bell-shaped curve. It had settled in one area for some time, moved to an adjacent area for what I suspect to be its first nesting attempt, and then moved back to the original location for the rest of the season, where we located an active nest.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 4
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Despite what seemed like fairly stable space use, this bird has a distinctly rising tail at the end of the variogram. I know the end of variograms can typically be discounted, but the rising pattern also seems to be a signature of variograms indicating non-range resident behavior, which is why I want someone with more skilled eyes to take a look at it for me.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 5
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Same story as bird #4, although it did have a couple tracking sessions that were located somewhat farther from its area of core use than normal.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 6
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Despite having an asymptote, this bird did slightly shift its area of core use during its second nesting attempt, although it was closer to its initial core use area than some of the movements displayed by the other birds discussed above.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks in advance for any guidance you all can provide!
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Tyler
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

It should be a list of the top models. I've made a note to add an informative error message otherwise, but in the future that would result in a 3-level hierarchical model.
If the beta coefficients are being dropped from the top model, then please send me a minimal working example (list of top fit objects should do it).

That warning means that some parameters are near a boundary and selection would likely drop them.
The NaNs could be from an unsupported parameter (can't differentiate the likelihood w.r.t.), which a rare category could give you. If this is the issue, then more merging of categories would be required.
The NaNs could be from a bad reference category. The reference category needs to be sampled in every dataset and not just in every UD. If you require different reference categories within a population, then I can move that feature up in priority. As of now, mean() needs the same reference category.

Best,
Chris

For this comparison, I am using effect size ratios rather than P-values as recommended by the Flemming et al. 2022 paper (Population‐level inference for home‐range areas - Fleming - 2022 - Methods in Ecology and Evolution - Wiley Online Library <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13815>). I find effect size ratios to be intuitive and easy to interpret. However, my first question relates to producing effect sizes for the confidence intervals: am I correct in thinking that to obtain the appropriate CIs for the effect sizes, you compare the ratios for the lower and upper bounds as you would the space use estimate itself?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > For the habitat selection analysis, we are planning to utilize a conventional approach to compare selection between the 95% home range and 50% core use areas (more discussion on this in a moment). Is it more appropriate to use the average UDs for this, or the individual stationary ranges? I know the iRSF approach implemented in ctmm requires the individual ranges since everything is contingent on the stationary movement models, but I imagine differences would be expected when using the individual versus average UDs in a conventional analysis as well. The UD contours appear very similar when comparing the average versus overlain individual ranges, but not exact.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Lastly, while reading other threads on RSFs in the group, I noticed that Chris and Jesse (and probably others) are now discouraging RSFs that compare different contours (e.g. 95% and 50%), despite this being a common practice in the literature and a goal of my own study. I think Jesse stated that the reasons for this are two-fold: 1) that it creates statistical challenges and 2) it creates philosophical issues by excluding some of the used locations from the analysis. I was hoping for more discussion and insight into why this practice is now being discouraged so I have a better grasp on the issue as I move into my own analysis (and thus can make better decisions). I read the recent iRSF paper (Mitigating pseudoreplication and bias in resource selection functions with autocorrelation‐informed weighting - Alston - 2023 - Methods in Ecology and Evolution - Wiley Online Library <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025>)- which was very eye-opening- and I intend to utilize it for future analyses, but because a goal of this study has always been to compare selection between the 95% and 50% contours, I was still hoping to use a conventional approach. I'm looking forward to more insight on this issue.

Hi Chris,

Thank you very much for providing potential solutions to my questions. I am trying to rerun the model with IC= "BIC" and will let you know if the problem is not solved.

Regarding your explanation about the mean() result, I want to clarify that while it indicates the best-fit model at the population level, it may not necessarily be the optimal model for each individual. Additionally, I found that mean() dropped some variables I specified in the model, contrary to the expectation that it should retain all variables. I have shared a link to the Dropbox folder via email. Please let me know if there are any issues with the files, and correct me if I misunderstood any details.

I have another question regarding the rsf.selection function: How can I "manually select the same reference category for each individual" when performing rsf.select? For example, can I specify category 1 as the reference category?

Thank you again for your help!

Best regards,

Fang

On Friday, February 2, 2024 at 4:03:29 PM UTC-5 Christen Fleming wrote:
> Hi Fang,
>
> Unlike AIC, AICc can potentially return infinite or NaN values if the number of parameters is not sufficiently larger than the number of data points (or effective-sample-size with rsf.fit). I suspect that is what you are getting, especially given that your species tends to have small effective sample sizes. I would try BIC and if that doesn't work, then please send me a minimal working example to check.
>
> mean() is coded up to provide a meta-analytic model for the population (and I just pushed a fix for that function for when the individual models vary). But you shouldn't expect one best individual model for all individuals, because, all else equal, the sampling can differ.
>
> rsf.select() can drop variables at the individual level, but mean() should then keep all of the variables in the individual selected models (though not all parameters will support estimation of the population variance). If that's not the case, then please send me a minimal working example to diagnose.
>
> You can supply different rasters for the suitability predictions than you did for the model fitting... if that's what you are asking?
>
> I haven't yet coded up the categorical regression to be smart at the population level. Currently, you need to manually select the same reference category for each individual. But that may not be possible if there is no single category that all individuals sample from. At some point, I need to code up the mean() function to automatically transform between reference categories. If you need that functionality now, then please let me know and I will prioritize it.
>
> For the error, please send me a minimal working example and I will take a look at it.
>
> Best,
> Chris

messages.subject: Beginner questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I've just finished watching the variogram and home range tutorials on Animove and am still wrapping my head around the subject (thank you so much for supplying such helpful educational tools). I successfully ran the code on a couple test individuals and now want to get the analysis underway on my entire dataset (n  = 23 individuals, 74k locations).

I have a few fundamental questions I was hoping you could assist with to help get me underway please.
Some individuals are seasonal migrants but only spend ~3 months away from their breeding home ranges (so range-resident 9 months of the year). Is there any issue with limiting the timespan of analysis to the breeding season to increase the study sample size by including these migrants?
Pertaining to question above - some individuals were also tagged as juveniles and either commenced breeding in second-third year or appeared to establish a home range by year 2. Prior to this they dispersed widely and meandered during their first-year. Can I subset these individuals from their first-year onwards to disregard juvenile movements or will the variogram pick up range-residency after this time period anyways and I can include these individuals in home range analysis?
Most of the tracking data is GPS data with a regular sampling schedule, but a smaller proportion are satellite (Argos) data with an irregular sampling schedule. Just checking that by treating these data individually (e.g. use weighted AKDE for satellite data but defaults for GPS) that home range estimates will still be comparable?
Is it possible/acceptable to calculate home ranges per individual per year? We have had individuals shift territories (e.g. breeding females swapping partners) between years, and also have interesting analysis to do regarding potential home range size shift for individuals in areas undergoing habitat loss (e.g. is home range size increasing as useable space decreases?) which would necessitate annual home range calculation.
Once again, thank you.
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Beginner questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

1. It depends on what you want (biologically) out of your (statistical) home range estimate. If you want to calculate area requirements, for example, cutting out the migratory period would clearly underestimate the area needed by the migratory animals. If you want to compare the areas used by a set of animals in a protected area, though, this might be fine.

2. You should subset to times when an animal has a stationary (unchanging) movement pattern. An assumption of AKDE right now is that an animal's movement pattern is the same across the entire time period of the training data, so including time periods when an animal is doing something different can create a bad statistical estimate.

3. We recommend always using the weighted AKDE unless it is computationally infeasible. But yes, one advantage of AKDEs is that they are comparable across all kinds of different data. That is often/usually not true of other estimators.

4. Again, because an assumption of the AKDE model is that an animal has a stationary movement pattern, if the animal is doing something different from year to year, then you should be subsetting by year. If the animal is maintaining a stationary home range, the estimates between years will essentially overlap and small differences in the home range will not be biologically meaningful.

Hope this is helpful.

Jesse

messages.body_plain:
Hi Fang,

Sorry for the delayed response, I'm teaching a new population ecology class.

There is a reference argument in rsf.fit() (which rsf.select will pass).  reference="auto" will choose the most frequent category as the reference category, but mean() currently requires the reference categories all to be the same. I can code up mean() to transform between reference categories automatically if and when someone needs that, which would be the case when there's no common category across individuals, as the reference category needs to be a used category.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Outlier and model fitting
messages.body_plain:
Hi Feipeng,

Sorry for the delay. The 200-meter filter is definitely too strong, as it leaves you with a visible circle around the geometric median. The only distance outliers I could potentially see are the cluster of northern most points, but that could easily be a place that the bird actually visited, as there are several points there. Otherwise, I don't see a clear need for distance-based filtering.

With the larger speed point estimates, I'm curious as to how low their lower CI limit goes (is it plausible?). I also don't know what the biological speed limit is for this age/species. Visually, I don't see anything sticking out of the speeds, but you might turn the transparency up to see better. One issue I've seen with some radio telemetry networks is underestimated error ellipses, which results in an overall increase in speed estimates and decrease in autocorrelation timescale estimates. Are your chicks really moving ~25 km/day in short 10-15 second trips? Do you have any test/calibration data for the network?

With the variogram, I'd look if it keeps increasing in the second half (6-12 days) and if that corresponds to a weekly shift or expansion in their range.

best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Plotting variograms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

For a facet-style plot in base plot, I usually just adjust par(mfrow).

The units on most all plots and summaries are automated for readability unless units=FALSE. The SVF y-axis could be in m^2, hectares, or km^2 depending on the size of the numbers.

Chris

I am trying to get a handle on whether a full season analysis may be possible and appropriate with these birds, and if a mean breeding season home range size would be usable to inform other aspects of the study and analysis (e.g., I want to use the mean home range size to create a biologically meaningful buffer distance in which to summarize habitat covariates for point-counts conducted on the same study sites). Below, I share the questionable variograms and briefly discuss each bird's space use.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Note: When I refer to "movements", these are often only on the scale of a few hundred meters.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 1
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > I was able to track this bird almost throughout the entire breeding season. At the beginning of the season, it had fairly static space use and was restricted to a small area, but during the post-fledging period its area of space use expanded greatly, and it was often found a few hundred meters from the area of original use. Then, during the post-breeding period, it briefly returned to its original area of use before settling in an area not too far from its original location. Despite this variable space use, however, the variogram seems rather stable.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 2
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > This bird had a very similar space use history to bird 1, with it occupying a fairly static area for much of the season, briefly moving away from this area during the post-fledging period, and then returning to the original location during the post-breeding period. However, rather the apparent asymptote of the first bird, this one has a distinct bell shape.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 3
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > This bird also has a bell-shaped curve. It had settled in one area for some time, moved to an adjacent area for what I suspect to be its first nesting attempt, and then moved back to the original location for the rest of the season, where we located an active nest.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 4
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Despite what seemed like fairly stable space use, this bird has a distinctly rising tail at the end of the variogram. I know the end of variograms can typically be discounted, but the rising pattern also seems to be a signature of variograms indicating non-range resident behavior, which is why I want someone with more skilled eyes to take a look at it for me.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 5
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Same story as bird #4, although it did have a couple tracking sessions that were located somewhat farther from its area of core use than normal.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Bird 6
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Despite having an asymptote, this bird did slightly shift its area of core use during its second nesting attempt, although it was closer to its initial core use area than some of the movements displayed by the other birds discussed above.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks in advance for any guidance you all can provide!
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Tyler
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

Warning: coercing argument of type 'list' to logicalError in mean.features(x, debias = debias, weights = weights, select = select, : 'list' object cannot be coerced to type 'logical'

Tyler

messages.subject: Implausible values from overlap()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,
  I was looking at the Bhattacharyya values from overlap and I am getting values that do not make sense. I get high BI values for individuals who do not have overlapping UDs. I have just started looking at the values for a single year and I have already found 2 cases out of four pairs.

I'm attaching plots of the UDs of these individuals and here are the associated values:

W0425 and W0621:
low: 0.55
est: 0.8
high: 0.97

W0713 and W0818:
low: 0.41
est: 0.66
high: 0.88

Here is the code I am using to get the overlaps & values into a dataframe:

ol_2013 <- overlap(uds_2013)
low_matrix <- ol_2013$CI[,,1]
est_matrix <- ol_2013$CI[,,2]
high_matrix <- ol_2013$CI[,,3]

overlap_df <- data.frame(ID1 = character(),
                         ID2 = character(),
                         low = numeric(),
                         est = numeric(),
                         high = numeric(),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

individuals <- rownames(low_matrix)

for (i in 1:nrow(low_matrix)) {
  for (j in 1:ncol(low_matrix)) {
    if (i < j) { # This ensures that each pair is only considered once
      overlap_df <- rbind(overlap_df, data.frame(ID1 = individuals[i],
                                                 ID2 = individuals[j],
                                                 low = low_matrix[i, j],
                                                 est = est_matrix[i, j],
                                                 high = high_matrix[i, j]))
    }
  }
}

Is this a bug or am I doing something wrong here? I have tried getting the values directly from the matrix and they're the same, e.g.

> est_matrix["W0425_2013", "W0621_2013"]
[1] 0.8012772

Let me know if you need me to send data/scripts to verify.

Thanks,
Jenny

Chris

I suppose my question was less about using a more complex model and more about using a less parameterized model (i.e. the null model). I was wondering if that should be the case with rsf.select() and mean(), as several birds have top models that have covariates but with the null in the competing set.

As always, thanks for the good discussions and assistance!

Tyler

It is possible to calculate an iRSF just by choosing a very large "available area" and then including the covariates x, y, x^2+y^2, but you also want to use importance sampling and sample from a pilot Gaussian for computational speed.
